headlines.title: Juvenile arrested after BB gun shot shatters window of Rohnert Park business
headlines.description: A juvenile was arrested Saturday afternoon after allegedly shooting at a business on Hunter Drive with a BB gun, shattering a window before authorities located him. The shooting occurred in the early afternoon of Saturday, when the Rohnert Park Department of Public Safety dispatch received a report of an unknown suspect shooting at a commercial building and fleeing in a vehicle, according to the Rohnert Park Police Department. A witness at the scene photographed the suspect vehicle, including its license plate. The shooting shattered a large glass window on the side of the business. Rohnert Park DPS patrol units began searching the area for the vehicle. Utilizing the Flock Automated License Plate Recognition camera system, a patrol unit located the vehicle a short time later and conducted a high-risk vehicle stop in a parking lot on Arlen Drive. Officers detained three juveniles and recovered a replica Glock-style BB gun inside the vehicle. One of the juveniles was ultimately arrested and booked into the Los Guilicos Juvenile Detention Center on charges of felony vandalism and displaying an imitation firearm in public.

headlines.title: Santa Rosa man arrested following Windsor vehicle pursuit in alleged stolen truck
headlines.description: A 32-year-old Santa Rosa man was arrested Monday morning after leading law enforcement on a vehicle pursuit in an allegedly stolen pickup truck through the Town of Windsor and along Highway 101, police said. Penrotana Yath was taken into custody without incident after deputies used a tire deflation device to stop the vehicle. No injuries were reported. The incident began at approximately 6:30 a.m. Monday, when Windsor Police deputies received a report of a stolen pickup truck. Using an Automated License Plate Recognition camera system, deputies located the truck a short time later traveling southbound on Highway 101 near central Windsor. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, Yath accelerated and fled, initiating a pursuit through town. A deputy attempted a Pursuit Intervention Technique maneuver to stop the vehicle, but the maneuver was unsuccessful and the driver continued fleeing. The pursuit traveled north of Windsor before Yath turned around and re-entered southbound Highway 101. A Sonoma County Sheriff’s Office sergeant deployed Stop Sticks near the Bicentennial Way overcrossing, puncturing one of the truck’s tires and slowing the vehicle until it came to a safe stop. The stolen pickup truck was recovered and returned to its registered owner. Yath was booked into the Sonoma County Jail on charges of vehicle theft, felony evading a peace officer, possession of a stolen vehicle, possession of burglary tools, violation of a court order and felony theft with priors.

headlines.title: Crash and vehicle fire shut down portion of Interstate 580 in Alameda County
headlines.description: A portion of Interstate 580 in Alameda County was shut down Monday afternoon due to a crash and vehicle fire, the California Highway Patrol said. The incident was reported on eastbound I-580 at the I-205 split. Caltrans advised motorists to avoid the area and use alternate routes Aerial coverage from NBC Bay Area’s SkyRanger at around 2 p.m. showed heavy traffic in the area and lanes on the freeway appeared to have been reopened. No other information was immediately available. This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

headlines.title: 1 of 2 canoers found dead in Tomales Bay identified as San Francisco man
headlines.description: Authorities said Monday that one of two people who died after a canoeing trip in Tomales Bay over the weekend was a San Francisco resident. Casey Flynn Melia, 36, and a companion who hasn’t been identified left their campsite on the bay in a canoe just before midnight on Saturday, according to the Marin County Sheriff’s Office. Fire officials said the pair had left to view bioluminescence in Tomales Bay, a narrow ocean inlet that separates Point Reyes peninsula from the rest of Marin County. When they didn’t return the following morning to their camp at White Gulch Beach, members of their camping group alerted authorities. Melia was found unresponsive on Sunday near Hog Island, a small island in Tomales Bay. He was recovered by the National Park Service and brought to Sacramento Landing, where first responders pronounced him dead. A short time before Melia was found, a search-and-rescue operation located the other canoer unresponsive in the water and they were rescued by the U.S. Coast Guard and transported to Bodega Bay in Sonoma County and declared dead. The Sonoma County Sheriff-Coroner Bureau is leading the investigation into the person’s death. A forensic post-mortem examination and routine toxicology testing are scheduled for later this week. The official cause and manner of death remain pending, awaiting the final findings of a joint investigation conducted by the Marin County Sheriff’s Office, the Coast Guard and the park service.

headlines.title: Home of Chicken and Waffles in Oakland to close after 23 years
headlines.description: Home of Chicken and Waffles in Oakland is closing its doors after 23 years. The restaurant’s owner said he’s ready to retire from the restaurant industry and move on to a new chapter. The last day of business is Monday. The restaurant moved about two years ago to its current location in Jack London Square. This marks the neighborhood’s second recent high-profile restaurant closure, following Plank one month ago.

headlines.title: Highway 101 weekend closure in San Francisco: Timeline and detour information
headlines.description: A portion of Highway 101 in San Francisco will shut down over two weekends in September as part of an ongoing pavement repair project, Caltrans said. Here’s what to know about the project, when the shutdowns will happen and detour information. When will Highway 101 shut down in San Francisco? The weekend shutdowns of northbound Highway 101 (Hospital Curve) will be held: 11 p.m. Friday, Sept. 4 through 6 a.m. Monday, Sept. 7 (Labor Day weekend) 11 p.m. Friday, Sept. 18 through 6 a.m. Monday, Sept. 21 What part of Highway 101 will be impacted by the pavement repair project? Caltrans will close all northbound Highway 101 lanes between Cesar Chavez and 10th streets. All southbound lanes will remain open. Detour information during Highway 101 closure in San Francisco Interstate 280 will be the main alternative during the northbound Hwy. 101 closure. Caltrans said I‑280 northbound is suggested for travel toward downtown San Francisco or the Bay Bridge. Public transportation is also highly encouraged to bypass congestion and avoid work‑zone delays. Why is a pavement repair project needed on Highway 101? The weekend closures along northbound Highway 101 in San Francisco is needed to complete pavement repair as part of a Hospital Curve rehabilitation project, Caltrans said. The project began in Fall 2025. Bay Area Aug 21 Transportation Jul 20

headlines.title: A decade after Colin Kaepernick took a knee that led to his exile, the ripple effects continue
headlines.description: Nothing about Colin Kaepernick, the football player, changed on that warm Southern California night a decade ago. Not his speed. Not his arm strength. Not the improvisational skills that made him one of the NFL’s most electrifying, if at times erratic, quarterbacks. And to be honest, nothing changed about Colin Kaepernick, the 28-year-old man, that night either. If anything, the moment the San Francisco 49ers star decided to take a knee during the national anthem before a preseason game on Sept. 1, 2016, to bring attention to a series of social issues he cares deeply about — from racial injustice to minority oppression to police brutality — only revealed to the world at large who Kaepernick always believed himself to be. “It wasn’t a sudden act,” he wrote in a statement this spring announcing his memoir, ”The Perilous Fight,” a title borrowed from a passage of the very song to which his name will forever be linked. No, it wasn’t. That night wasn’t even the first time the player who always seemed to have one eye on the field and the other on the world at large chose to do something other than stand during the anthem. In the two previous 49er exhibitions that August, he sat on the bench, largely unnoticed, as the anthem played. Only after connecting with former NFL player and retired Green Beret Nate Boyer in a hotel lobby did Kaepernick move from the bench to a knee, something Boyer suggested would be more respectful to those in the military. He didn’t announce he was going to do it. He didn’t share it on social media. He didn’t promote it in any way. He just did it, quietly placing his right knee on the ground, his left arm across his left knee and staring silently ahead as Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Steven Powell sang “The Star-Spangled Banner.” When Kaepernick huddled with noted sociologist and then-49ers advisor Harry Edwards in the aftermath, they both knew Kaepernick’s decision carried considerable risk. While Kaepernick, who is biracial, was hardly the first athlete of color to parlay the playing of the anthem into an attempt to draw attention to social inequity — from U.S. track athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos at the 1968 Summer Olympics to college basketball player Ariyana Smith at Knox College, who in late 2014 stood under the basket with her hands up during the anthem, then laid on the court for over four minutes in protest over the shooting death of Black teenager Michael Brown in Missouri — Edwards understood the spotlight the NFL provides and Kaepernick’s status within the game had the potential to make it a divisive cultural flashpoint. “I said, ‘You know, this is going to become a major issue,’” Edwards told The Associated Press. “You are a Black male and seen as a greater threat because of the centrality of male activities and male sports. And so there’s no way that there’s not going to be a price to pay for this.” The price ended up being Kaepernick’s football career. The conversation Kaepernick intended to start was instead hijacked. The method of Kaepernick’s protest became the focus, with critics calling it offensive, particularly to those in the armed forces. Then-Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump lashed out and later, as president, labeled any player who knelt a “son of a bitch”. Fans burned Kaepernick’s jersey in anger. The boos that cascaded in his direction every Sunday were hardly limited to 49er road games, though the franchise trudging through a miserable 2-14 season didn’t help. While supporters pointed out that Kaepernick’s right to kneel is one of the freedoms protected by the First Amendment of the Constitution, the very thing those in uniform are commanded to defend, it didn’t seem to matter. No matter how hard Kaepernick kept trying to steer the talk toward racial injustice, it swerved in seemingly every other direction instead. Four months after kneeling for the first time, Kaepernick threw his 1,692nd and final pass in the NFL, a 9-yard touchdown pass to tight end Garrett Celek late in the fourth quarter against Seattle, a play that highlighted some of what made Kaepernick so tantalizing as a player. He dropped back, glanced to his left, then stepped up in the pocket and fired a dart over the middle to Celek in the end zone. The score brought the 49ers to within three. San Francisco never got the ball again. The Seahawks ran out the clock, and Kaepernick’s No. 7 jersey disappeared down the tunnel toward the locker room one last time. The 49ers hit reboot during the offseason, firing head coach Chip Kelly and replacing him with Kyle Shanahan. Kaepernick met with Shanahan and new general manager John Lynch, then opted to void the remaining year on his contract and become a free agent. The player whose rise in 2012 sparked San Francisco to an NFC title, who once led former NFL quarterback-turned-analyst Ron Jaworski to wonder aloud if Kaepernick could become one of the best ever at the position, never pulled on a uniform again. Kaepernick and former teammate Eric Reid — who knelt alongside him in 2016 — filed a lawsuit against the NFL claiming owners colluded to blacklist them out of the game. A settlement was reached in 2019, and while Kaepernick kept one toe in the game — as late as 2022, he worked out for the Las Vegas Raiders — both he and the league seem to have moved on. An absence that still leaves some wondering ‘why’? Nearing 10 years after the 72nd and final touchdown pass of his career, the circumstances remain hard for some to square. How is it that 32 teams saw a player in his prime, a player who guided a team to the Super Bowl, and who was only a couple of years removed from leading his team on a pair of deep playoff runs, and decided “nah, we’re good”? The NFL is, in just about every way, a meritocracy. Pedigree doesn’t matter, only production. The league’s history is filled with players granted countless second (and in some cases, third or fourth) chances despite various misdeeds, some of whom returned to the field after spending time in prison. Over the last month, the Seattle Seahawks sprinted to land cornerback Terrion Arnold even as he faces eight felony charges stemming from an incident in Florida. Arnold, who has denied the allegations, agreed to a one-year deal on Saturday and was immediately placed on the commissioner’s exempt list by the NFL while it conducts its own investigation. Kaepernick, by contrast, remains unsigned to this day even as countless quarterbacks with lesser resumes have drifted in and out of the league. His exile doesn’t quite make sense to longtime Pittsburgh Steelers defensive lineman Cam Heyward. Heyward described Kaepernick as “hell of a talent” who created “headaches” for opponents on the field and who once passed for 302 yards, ran for 62 more, and accounted for a pair of touchdowns in the Super Bowl, a game Heyward is still waiting to play in as he enters his 16th season. Heyward, a seven-time Pro Bowler and the league’s 2023 recipient of the Walter Payton Man of the Year award for his charity work and contributions to the community off the field, also remembers a player who stuck to his convictions in the face of withering pressure. The way Heyward figures it, isn’t that kind of the point? While stressing he didn’t have all the specifics on why Kaepernick never played again, Heyward said the quiet part out loud when asked if he felt Kaepernick’s stand was the driving force behind why he didn’t play beyond 2016. “I don’t think any player deserves that,” Heyward told the AP. “I think we all strive to be football players, but then we also strive to give back. And you never would think it would lead to that. It feels like he paid the price with his career. I just don’t think that’s right.” Even as football opportunities dried up, Kaepernick doubled down on his activism It’s telling of how fraught Kaepernick’s decision remains 10 years later that numerous people who either played or coached alongside Kaepernick in 2016 declined to speak to the AP about their experiences of that season and its fallout. “I think that this reluctance to even talk about it now is indicative of to what degree did the NFL substantively address it,” said Frederick Gooding Jr., a professor of African-American studies at TCU and the author of a book examining the intersection of race, media and sports. “If anything, people should be more open to talk about this, warts and all.” It hasn’t happened on the scale Kaepernick envisioned, and Gooding added that he believes one reason Kaepernick never took another snap was the way he “forced people to get uncomfortable.” It wasn’t until 2020, in the wake of George Floyd’s murder in Minnesota, that NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell acknowledged the league misstepped by not listening to players like Kaepernick who were fighting for social equality. By then, Kaepernick was already three-plus years removed from the sport. “Now that the game has been decided, now that his career is effectively over, now from a power and control standpoint, the NFL still is able to acknowledge that maybe they should have listened better, but they’re not losing anything,” Gooding said. “Now the stakes are lower for them to admit in retrospect.” While demonstrating during the anthem spread across the league in the immediate aftermath — with as many as 200 players taking a knee at times during the 2017 season — the temperature, at least inside NFL stadiums, has been turned down even as it remains ratcheted up in so many other areas of society. Edwards, whose roots in promoting social justice date back to his time counseling Smith and Carlos to raise their gloved fists in a Black power salute while on the medal stand at the 1968 Olympics, once publicly lobbied for Kaepernick to return to the game. Now, he sees the work Kaepernick and his wife, Nessa, have done through the years — from the “Know Your Rights” camps they host to promote “education, self-empowerment, mass-mobilization” for people of color to the independent autopsies their foundation pays for (most recently following the death of Black teenager Nolan Wells in Mississippi) — and believes the game would have just gotten in the way. “Nothing he would ever accomplish in football, even if there was a team that would bring him on board, would match his importance as a sports political figure in the first two decades of the 20th century,” Edwards said. “And I think that that’s critically important that that example be out there. There will be others who will come along. The only thing that’s missing today is that broad-scale societal movement that athletes use as scaffolding to make their statements.” Kaepernick’s activism inspired others from afar Marcellis Perkins watched intently from the other side of the country as the rhetoric around Kaepernick heated up. A sophomore forward on the Holy Cross men’s basketball team at the time, Perkins had long felt the pull of civic engagement while growing up in Hampton Roads, Virginia. An advisor, sensing a need for allyship in a particularly fraught environment, suggested to Perkins and a handful of other athletes that they start meeting regularly in an effort to carve out a place for them to openly share their experiences. During those early days the group, which became known as Men of Color Athletes (MOCA), would talk openly about Kaepernick’s commitment to his cause at a time it wasn’t unusual for them to hear criticism of the 49ers quarterback in their own locker rooms in Worcester, Massachusetts — a good 2,500 miles from San Francisco. “I’m like well, if our coach says this or the captain of the team says this, how can we feel like we express ourselves or find the words to talk about what’s actually happening from our perspective without feeling like we’ll be penalized?” Perkins said. “And so the best thing we could do is create a space for ourselves where we can talk and share these resources, share these thoughts and better equip ourselves.” Perkins, who now holds a doctorate in philosophy and is the program director for an entrepreneurship program at TCU, likened Kaepernick’s stand to ones made by predecessors Muhammad Ali and Jim Brown, only they were living through it, not reading about it in a book. In Kaepernick, the men in MOCA saw “somebody reflecting and representing us and using their voice.” What began with a group of around 10 athletes quickly grew into 30 and laid the foundation for a women’s group. An enduring example On a personal level, Perkins watched Kaepernick deftly navigate the transition from athlete to former athlete, a path Perkins had to walk himself when injuries forced him to spend his final years at Holy Cross watching from the sideline. Perkins has been heavily involved in several projects since moving to the Fort Worth area, including serving on a non-profit board that addresses health inequities and for a time, running an after-school program at an all-boys school. While Perkins has always felt pulled in this direction, Kaepernick provided more than a gentle nudge. It’s one of the many ways ACLU President Deborah Archer told the AP that Kaepernick’s journey “set an example” for others to follow. “He showed what they can do, the power that they have to start conversation,” she said after the organization presented Kaepernick with an activism award at a ceremony in Washington, D.C., in July. “For so long athletes, actors were told: That’s your lane, stay in your lane. He showed that there is no lane. We are all a part of this democracy, that we all have a right to speak, we all have an obligation to speak.” An obligation that Kaepernick is perhaps even more fervently committed to now at 38 than he was at 28. Yes, speaking out came at a high personal cost. And yes, there will always be a segment of the populace whose judgment of him will begin and end with the image of Kaepernick on one knee while someone sings about “the land of the free and the home of the brave.” No, he did not make it to the Hall of Fame as some once thought might be possible. Yet for those like Perkins who were inspired by watching someone take a stand at deep personal cost in hopes of creating what Edwards likes to call the quest for a “more perfect union,” it hardly matters. “I would hope and I would think that when he looks back on his legacy, he’ll say ‘I made the right decision because of all the lives that were impacted, all the lives that were changed,’ … that is a different level of greatness,” Perkins said. “The media might not celebrate it, but the people will. I think that’s all that matters.” ___ AP Sports Writers Alanis Thames, Kristie Rieken, Doug Ferguson, Mark Long, Terry Tang and Dan Gelston contributed to this report. ___ See AP’s full NFL coverage here

headlines.title: Ed Sheeran surprises fans during Pokémon World Championships at Chase Center
headlines.description: Ed Sheeran surprised Pokémon fans in San Francisco with a special performance as the Pokémon World Championships wrapped up Sunday night. The Grammy-winning singer took the stage at Chase Center to perform the Pokémon theme song during the final night of the three-day event. Tens of thousands of people descended on San Francisco over the weekend for the Pokémon fan convention and World Championships. The finals were held Sunday at Chase Center, with competitors vying for a share of $2 million in prizes. Andrew Hedrick, 20, was named this year’s Masters Division champion for the Pokémon Trading Card Game, while Takuma Yamazaki won the video game title. Several other winners also took home cash prizes. Outside Moscone Center, Howard Street was transformed into a fan fest for the three-day celebration. Next year’s Pokémon World Championships will be held in Singapore for the first time.’ San Francisco Aug 29 San Francisco Aug 28 San Francisco Giants Aug 27 San Francisco Giants welcome in Pokémon fans to a special game at Oracle Park

headlines.title: Volunteers rescue climber stranded on small ledge in California's Sierra Nevada
headlines.description: Volunteers carried out a more than 15-hour operation to rescue a man who got off route in the Sierra Nevada and was stranded on a small ledge, the Mono County Sheriff Search and Rescue Team said. A four-person team carried out the rescue last weekend near Mammoth Lakes, California, in a precarious gully. The challenge came in having no time to spare with thousands of feet of vertical exposure below, said team spokesperson Mitchell Quiring. The stranded climber had only one foot fully on the 6-inch ledge and was shaking out his legs and switching them to avoid tiring, said Quiring, who was part of the rescue team. “Any fall would almost certainly be fatal,” the team wrote on its Facebook page. Quiring said he credits the climber, Rob Martin, with having the strength and will to live. “He was not going to give up. He was going to push until there was a solution,” Quiring said. “It’s what we train for, so there’s a lot of trust in leaning back on that.” The volunteer group has long trained to carry out technical rescues. The rescuers are among those dispatched the Mono County Sheriff’s Office in the Sierra Nevada, about 200 miles east of San Francisco.

headlines.title: 2 people hurt after shooting on Highway 101 in San Carlos
headlines.description: A shooting injured two people and shut down a busy stretch of Highway 101 in San Carlos for hours Sunday, according to the California Highway Patrol. The shooting happened around 5 p.m. on northbound Highway 101 south of Holly Street, according to the CHP. Investigators said someone opened fire on a black Infiniti sedan carrying three people — a 25-year-old driver and passengers ages 22 and 17. It remains unclear whether the people inside the car were targeted or caught in the crossfire. One person was grazed by a bullet in the hand, while another suffered a back injury. No one was seriously injured. The shooting prompted officers to shut down northbound Highway 101 for hours, causing significant traffic backups. “I was stuck in traffic near Whipple. We weren’t moving. I was there for an hour and 45 minutes,” Daly City resident Carlos Palma told NBC Bay Area. All lanes have since reopened. The CHP has not identified a possible motive or released a description of the suspected gunman or vehicle. The investigation is ongoing. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates.

headlines.title: Man arrested after shootout near Manzanita Park in Oakland
headlines.description: A man was arrested after allegedly threatening to kill a woman and shooting at officers near Manzanita Park in Oakland on Sunday, police said. The police department said they received multiple 911 calls at 10:30 a.m. about a man threatening to kill a woman at Manzanita Park. Police arrived at the scene, and the suspect immediately began shooting at the officers, authorities said. Officials said the officers returned fired and the suspect fled to the neighborhood. Authorities added the woman was rescued and taken to a safe place. Oakland PD set up a command center inside the perimeter, which encompassed the Manzanita Park neighborhood. Authorities said the suspect hid at an abandoned home in the 2600 block of 22nd Avenue. Just before 3 p.m., the suspect lit items on fire, threw them at officers and set the home ablaze. “During that process he started throwing flammable cans, that he lit on fire, at police officers, and he lit the building that he was in on fire. The officers had to emergency deploy smoke, to get him to exit the building, at which point our canine-tactical team took him into custody,” Oakland Police Department Chief James Beere said. Police said the suspect exited the house and fought officers as they tried to take him into custody. The suspect was taken to an Oakland hospital for injuries sustained in the arrest, according to the police department. Beere said investigators believe the gunman knew the woman rescued by officers.. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates.

headlines.title: Suspect in deadly Oakland stabbing spree expected in court
headlines.description: The man accused of killing one person and injuring four others in a stabbing spree across Oakland is expected to appear before a judge Monday. Jose Rodriguez, 34, was scheduled to be arraigned Friday, but the hearing was postponed after he refused to get on a bus at Santa Rita Jail for the trip to court in Oakland, according to Alameda County Superior Court. Rodriguez is accused of stabbing five people at several locations across Oakland last Monday. Police said the attacks began at Cesar Chavez Park and spanned about a mile through East Oakland. One of the victims, 58-year-old Gonzalo Lopez, died. His family said Lopez was going to get his bicycle fixed when he was killed in what they believe was a random attack. Rodriguez has a lengthy criminal history, including a conviction stemming from a 2019 stabbing spree in which he stabbed an Uber driver and a garbage collector. He was eventually released on parole, but court records show he repeatedly violated his parole. Those violations include an arrest in June 2025 for assault and violating a criminal protective order filed by his father. NBC Bay Area’s Bob Redell has the full report in the video above.
